title: Local anaesthetic | NHS inform
text:
Local anaesthetic
Local anaesthesia involves numbing an area of the body and you remain awake.
What is local anaesthetic used for?
Local anaesthetic can be used to:
treat pain
prevent pain during a procedure or operation
relieve pain after surgery
Treating pain
Gels and sprays that contain local anaesthetic can sometimes be used to treat
mouth ulcers
and
sore throats
.
Local anaethetic injections and
steroid medication
may be used to treat more severe conditions. For example, long-term joint pain.
Preventing pain
Local anaesthetic is usually used to prevent pain during a minor procedure or operation such as:
a filling
wisdom tooth removal
removal of moles,
warts or verrucas
some types of eye surgery like cataract removal
a
biopsy
Local anaethetic may be used during major surgery if you need to be awake. For example, certain types of brain surgery.
Local anaethetic may also be used to prevent pain after a major operation is carried out under a
general anaesthetic
.
Epidural and spinal anaesthetics
An
epidural anaesthetic
is where a local anaesthetic is injected through a tube into the lower back. This procedure is often called an epidural.
A spinal anaesthetic is a single injection into a similar space in the back.
Epidural and spinal anaesthetics can be used:
during
childbirth
to ease the pain of labour, or if a caesarean section is needed
to reduce the amount of general anaesthetic needed during some operations and to prevent pain after
instead of a general anaesthetic in some types of surgery, like knee and
hip replacements
Peripheral nerve blocks
A nerve block is an injection of a local anaesthetic to numb the nerves supplying a particular part of the body. This could be the hand, arm or leg. It may be used instead of general anaesthetic for certain operations and can prevent pain after.
An
ultrasound scan
is often used to pinpoint the correct nerve. The injection shouldn’t be painful.
How local anaesthetic works
Local anaesthetic stops the nerves in a part of your body from sending signals to your brain.
You won’t be able to feel any pain after having a local anaesthetic. You may still feel some pressure or movement.
It usually takes a few minutes to lose feeling in the area where a local anaesthetic is given. Feeling should return a few hours later when the medication has worn off.
Types of local anaesthetic
Depending on what it’s being used for, local anaesthetic can be given as:
injections
creams
gels
sprays
ointments
How local anaesthetic is given
Local anaesthetic is usually given by:
dentists
surgeons
anaesthetists
GPs
other doctors
You may be given a sedative as well as local anaesthetic to keep you relaxed during a procedure or operation.
Some medications containing mild local anaesthetic are available on prescription. They may also be available over the counter from pharmacies. Ask your pharmacist for advice on the right treatment for you if you’re on any medication.
Possible side effects
Some people experience temporary side effects from a local anaesthetic. These problems will usually pass. You should tell your healthcare professional if you experience any side effects.
Common side effects
Common side effects of local anaesthetic include:
dizziness
headaches
blurred vision
twitching muscles
continuing numbness
weakness
pins and needles
Less common side effects
In very rare cases, you could:
have an allergic reaction to the local anaesthetic
develop serious problems like seizures (fits)
have a cardiac arrest (when the heart stops pumping blood around the body)
Warnings and precautions
Local anaesthetic can cause:
discomfort when the injection is given
a tingling sensation as the medication wears off
minor bruising, bleeding or soreness where the injection was given
You should move carefully until the anaesthetic has worn off. This is because you may not notice if you’ve injured yourself.
